articles.title: AI Image Guides for Small Teams: Build a One-Page Visual Spec So Every Contributor Ships Consistent Assets
articles.excerpt: If three different people make images for your project, you will get three different visual identities within a month. One person likes moody lighting, another reaches for bright flat colors, and the…
articles.body: If three different people make images for your project, you will get three different visual identities within a month. One person likes moody lighting, another reaches for bright flat colors, and the third copies whatever looked good on social media that week. Searching for ai image guides usually means you have hit this wall: each image is fine on its own, but together they look like they came from three unrelated brands. The fix is not a thicker brand book. It is a small, living document I call an AI image guide: a one-page visual spec plus a prompt and reference playbook that anyone on the team can follow without asking you. This article walks through how to build one, with three concrete examples, and is honest about what a guide can and cannot control.
articles.author: Jay

articles.title: Orchestrator and Sub-Agent Patterns: Designing Specialist Agents That Collaborate
articles.excerpt: In one sentence: Splitting work among specialist agents is only the start; the craft lies in choosing the right collaboration pattern (router, pipeline, fan-out, planner, reviewer or human checkpoint)…
articles.body: In one sentence: Splitting work among specialist agents is only the start; the craft lies in choosing the right collaboration pattern (router, pipeline, fan-out, planner, reviewer or human checkpoint) for each part of the job and in giving every pattern clear contracts and firm limits. Once a team accepts that one agent is rarely enough, a new question appears: how should the specialists work together? The answer is not a single architecture. Different problems call for different collaboration patterns and choosing badly produces agents that loop, duplicate effort or argue in circles. This post is a practical catalog. We use the STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result) to show how ad hoc collaboration fails and how a small set of well-understood patterns replaces it.

articles.body: You need the pages of a website, but you don't know its URLs yet. On sitemap vs crawl, the short answer is this. Read the sitemap when you only need the URLs a site chooses to publish. Use Map when you need the site's URLs and the sitemap isn't enough. Use Crawl when you need the pages themselves and can describe them. This post gives you a decision tree and shows what each method returns on real sites, with code you can repeat. What each method gives you All three discover pages, but they answer different questions: Read the sitemap yourself A sitemap is a file the site publishes, so reading it is free and takes one request per file.

articles.title: I built a browser test that proves when a mouse sensor loses tracking (and got my refund with it)
articles.excerpt: Short story long, I bought a budget gaming mouse and something felt off in Valorant: slow aiming was fine, but hard flicks moved the crosshair far less than my hand did, and sometimes it snapped backw…
articles.body: Short story long, I bought a budget gaming mouse and something felt off in Valorant: slow aiming was fine, but hard flicks moved the crosshair far less than my hand did, and sometimes it snapped backwards. The usual online mouse testers check buttons, double-clicks and polling rate. None of them could show the seller what was actually happening. So I built one that can. The idea If the mouse moves the exact same physical distance every time, a healthy sensor reports the same number of counts, no matter how fast you move. So: Put two hard stops on the mousepad (books, a ruler, the pad's edges). Do a few slow swipes between them. Their median becomes the baseline. Flick hard between the same stops.

articles.title: We Plugged an LLM Into Our Review Pipeline - And Built It So the Model Can Never Decide
articles.excerpt: We Plugged an LLM Into Our Review Pipeline - And Built It So the Model Can Never Decide Short answer: our agents file feedback and request human review shadow means the model works blind and supervise…
articles.body: We Plugged an LLM Into Our Review Pipeline - And Built It So the Model Can Never Decide Short answer: our agents file feedback and request human review (EPIC-230), and humans were doing all the sorting, reading, and drafting by hand. So we wired an LLM into six operator scenarios - classification, summaries, knowledge search, answer drafts, feedback extraction, review hints - under four modes where shadow means the model works blind and supervised still ends with a human pressing the button. The decision table has no code path an AI run can write to. Every mode change, every call, and every cent of spend lands in append-only rows you can audit. This is part of the Arc campaign series. Previous published episode: a keyless agent protocol with signed webhooks (EPIC-233).

articles.title: I built a free Google Play keyword rank checker (no sign-up). Here is how it works
articles.excerpt: Why I publish Android apps and wanted one number per keyword, per country, per day, without buying a full ASO suite. So I built Rankfy. For Google Play, Rankfy requests the public search page for a ke…
articles.body: Why I publish Android apps and wanted one number per keyword, per country, per day, without buying a full ASO suite. So I built Rankfy. How it works For Google Play, Rankfy requests the public search page for a keyword with the country ( gl ) and language ( hl ) set, and reads the apps in the order the store returns them. For the App Store, it uses the public iTunes Search API with the country code. Your position is your index in that list. A scheduled job repeats the check every day and stores the history. No paid data source is involved, which is why it cannot tell you search volume. What surprised me Positions move within a day. One weather app was #27 in the morning and #8 at night for the same keyword. Country and store language matter more than I expected.

articles.excerpt: Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.
articles.body: Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star. That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao. A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii.

articles.title: 'Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home' at 40: 'Trek' has never been as joyous or fun as in 'the one with the whales'
articles.excerpt: Colorful metaphors, a near-miss with Eddie Murphy and humpback whales in 20th-century California.
articles.body: It may have been subtitled "The Voyage Home", but to most viewers "Star Trek IV" (which has just turned 40) will always be "the one with the whales". After "The Wrath of Khan" and "The Search for Spock" went to some pretty dark places — ear worms, the destruction of the Enterprise, the death (and later resurrection) of a certain beloved Vulcan — the franchise was in need of some light relief. So what better than to set coordinates for the then-present day of 1986 San Francisco, for a time-travel comedy romp? Spock himself, Leonard Nimoy, had directed "The Search for Spock" and Paramount had lined him up to call the shots on a follow-up before the movie had even landed in theaters.
